chunks: "When the switch opens, the inductor current can't stop instantly, so the inductor voltage reverses and the switch node flies up.
In a boost the diode catches it: once the node gets to the output voltage plus a diode drop, the diode turns on, and the inductor current flows into the output capacitor and load.
So the flyback voltage is clamped at V out plus V F , and instead of being a spike it becomes the normal off-state voltage on the switch. That's why it's important in two ways.
It's the working principle: the inductor's flyback energy is what gets delivered to the output at a higher voltage.
And it sets the stress on the switch, which has to withstand at least V out plus some ringing margin. The dangerous case is when the current has nowhere to go.
If the diode is open, the energy goes into the tiny node capacitance and the voltage rises as I square root of L over C . With 1. 5 amps, 4.
7 microhenries and 100 picofarads on the node, that's over 300 volts, far above a 20 volts FET.
And if the load is removed with nothing limiting the output, the output capacitor gets pumped up a little every cycle until something breaks.
That's why boost controllers have overvoltage protection and why you look at the switch node on a scope for overshoot and ringing."
